entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency and NGVL (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2328
entry.content:
The Guidance and Appeals Panel reviewed an ART decision that had found funding for an Orangutan Plus Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories to be a reasonable and necessary NDIS support for NGVL, a child with Autism and ADHD. The Panel focused on whether the equipment was “standard indoor or outdoor play equipment” excluded by item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules.

Key holding: Standard outdoor play equipment falling within item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules is not an NDIS support and cannot be funded unless it is modified or adapted to address the participant’s functional impairments.

For the reasons given below, the Panel concludes that the Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories are 'standard...outdoor play equipment' and are therefore an excluded support under item 4(p) in Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules. On this basis it cannot be included for funding in NGVL's SOPS.

entry.title: Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 213
entry.content:
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.

Key holding: Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

entry.title: South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2304
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).

Key holding: Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. It follows that, in 2024, those students were in the foundation year of schooling, were receiving primary education and were therefore primary students at their school.

entry.title: Tran and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2300
entry.content:
Mr Tran sought review of ASQA’s decision to cancel his Certificate III in Carpentry, obtained via RPL from Kingsway, a deregistered RTO. Although the Tribunal found the s 56(1)(a) ground was established because Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary assessment, it exercised the discretion not to cancel in exceptional circumstances. The cancellation decision was set aside and the qualification is to be treated as a valid VET RPL qualification.

Key holding: Even when the s 56(1)(a) ground is established, the Tribunal may exercise the s 56(1) discretion not to cancel a VET qualification in exceptional circumstances, including clear lack of applicant fault, misleading RTO conduct, extensive genuine industry experience, and a public interest that does not require cancellation.

The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. That discretion may be exercised consistent with the public interest, given that Mr Tran possesses the requisite training, skills and work experience to have been awarded the Qualification on an RPL basis.

entry.title: Niven and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2274
entry.content:
This was a merits review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Niven’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the applicant did not pass the character test but accepted there was another reason to revoke the cancellation, set aside the delegate’s decision, and substituted a decision revoking the cancellation.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal may revoke mandatory cancellation if satisfied there is another reason, applying Direction no. 110.

Section 501CA(4) states that the Minister may revoke the original decision if: (a) the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation; and (b) the Minister is satisfied: (i) that the person passes the character test (as defined by s 501); or (ii) that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Kintanar (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2384
entry.content:
In Kintanar (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2384, the Tribunal reviewed a refusal of a Partner (Temporary) (Class UK)/Subclass 820 visa because the applicant’s non-migrating child, Leonel, failed PIC 4007 due to severe cognitive impairment/autism and an estimated care cost of $1,577,840. The Tribunal found the MOC opinion valid but waived the health criterion under PIC 4007(2)(b), weighing the child’s non-migrating status, the applicant’s and sponsor’s regional NSW contributions, and their capacity to mitigate future costs.

Key holding: Under PIC 4007(2)(b), the Tribunal may waive the health criterion where the benefits and contributions of the applicant and sponsor, the detriment of refusal, and the applicant’s capacity to mitigate future costs outweigh a cost that cannot be realised from the grant of the visa alone.

The Tribunal concludes that the benefits that the visa applicant and her partner bring to the Australian community, the detriment to the visa sponsor and his family if the visa was refused and the applicant and sponsor's capacity to mitigate the potential costs to the Australia community should Leonel apply for a visa in the future to join his mother, outweigh a cost to the Australian community which cannot be realised from the grant of this visa alone.

entry.title: Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275
entry.content:
In Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275, a 31-year-old New Zealand citizen who has lived in Australia since infancy had his special category visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 7 years 6 months for serious drug offences. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, but the Administrative Review Tribunal set that decision aside and substituted revocation after finding “another reason” under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Key holding: Under Direction no. 110, whether a non-citizen poses an “unacceptable risk” is a distinct evaluative conclusion reached by balancing the likelihood and potential harm of future offending, not merely the likelihood of re-offending.

The concept of 'risk', and whether it is 'unacceptable', under cl 8.1.2(1) of the Direction is not the same thing as the 'likelihood of the non-citizen engaging in further criminal or other serious conduct'.[25]

entry.title: Al-Hajj and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2318
entry.content:
Mr Al-Hajj sought review of the NDIA’s decision about the statement of participant supports in his NDIS plan, contending for 24/7 1:1 support worker assistance and weekly psychology. The ART considered whether those supports were reasonable and necessary under s 34(1) of the NDIS Act and related rules. It set aside the decisions and remitted the matter with orders for 3 hours/day daily personal activities, 2 hours/day community participation, and 30 hours of psychology.

Key holding: Under s 34(1)(aa) of the NDIS Act, a support must be necessary to address needs arising directly from an impairment for which the participant meets the disability or early intervention requirements.

What follows from the above determination is that for the purposes of s 34(1)(aa), the supports sought on review must be necessary to address needs of Mr Al-Hajj arising directly from his psychosocial impairments.

entry.title: Austro Enterprises Pty Limited (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2379
entry.content:
Austro Enterprises Pty Limited sought review of a delegate’s refusal to approve a nomination for Mr Erich Martinez as Office Manager under the Core Skills stream of the Subclass 482 visa. The delegate found the position was not genuine under reg 2.72(10) because existing roles allegedly covered the duties. The Tribunal accepted the position was genuine and remitted the nomination for reconsideration.

Key holding: Whether a position is genuine under reg 2.72(10)(a) requires a qualitative, reality-tested comparison between the actual position and the nominated occupation, not merely paper duties.

Regulation 2.72(10)(a) requires that the position associated with the nominated occupation is genuine. A similar requirement was considered in Cargo First Pty Ltd v MIBP [2016] FCA 30, where the Court (at [34]) upheld the Tribunal's approach of qualitatively assessing the position and comparing this with the occupation nominated in order to determine whether it was genuine.

entry.title: FPXJ and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2321
entry.content:
The Applicant, FPXJ, sought an extension of time to bring second review applications in the Administrative Review Tribunal against two AAT first review decisions dated 19 August 2019 and 29 January 2020 concerning disability support pension debts. The Tribunal rejected his procedural and bias arguments and refused the extension. It found the delay exceeded six years, was not fully explained, and that reopening settled matters would prejudice the Respondent and wider public, with no practical utility in the substantive review.

Key holding: Under s 19 of the ART Act, the Tribunal may refuse an extension of time where significant delay, prejudice and lack of practical utility mean it is not reasonable in all the circumstances to extend time.

Given this, and given the prejudice to the Respondent and to the wider public if an extension of time is granted, the Tribunal has decided that it is not reasonable in all of the circumstances to extend time for the Applicant to make second review applications. The extension of time applications are refused by the Tribunal.

It set aside the refusal and remitted the application, finding his strong recent master’s results, family ties in India and the course’s value outweighed earlier concerns about course changes and slow completion.

entry.title: CUCCI (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2383
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal of a Subclass 500 (Student) visa on the basis that Mr Cucci was not a genuine temporary entrant under cl 500.212 of Schedule 2 to the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth). The Tribunal had considerably more evidence than the delegate and found that the applicant did intend genuinely to stay in Australia temporarily and to comply with visa conditions. entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming non-revocation of the applicant’s mandatorily cancelled Resident Return visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act. The Tribunal found the applicant failed the character test and that there was no another reason to revoke, but the Court held it failed to consider his non-refoulement claims as required by Ministerial Direction 110.
